about.title: Sunnyvale Workplace Injury Claims
about.longDescription: Sunnyvale's workday looks different depending on where you clock in. Some people spend it inside labs and office campuses off Mathilda Avenue, others on construction sites, in warehouses near SR-237, or behind the wheel making deliveries along El Camino Real and Fair Oaks Avenue. When a shift ends with an injury, the first step is usually a workers' compensation claim, which in California covers medical care and part of lost wages no matter who was at fault. What many injured workers in Santa Clara County do not hear is that comp may not be the whole story. If a subcontractor, a property owner, a defective piece of equipment, or another driver contributed to what happened, a separate third-party claim can sit alongside the comp case. That matters for anyone hurt driving for work, too; Sunnyvale recorded 457 injury collisions in 2025, and work trips are part of that picture. LawProactive helps you sort out which path applies. We connect you, free of charge, with an independent attorney who reviews your situation and works on contingency.

whyChoose.title: Why Sunnyvale Workers Start With LawProactive

items.title: We help you see past the comp claim
items.desc: Workers' compensation is usually your only remedy against your employer in California, but a negligent third party such as a subcontractor, property owner, or equipment maker can open a separate claim. An attorney in our network can look for that second path.

items.title: Deadlines are explained, not buried
items.desc: California expects you to report a workplace injury to your employer within 30 days, and a third-party injury claim generally carries a two-year filing deadline. We connect you quickly so those clocks do not run out unnoticed.

items.title: Retaliation has consequences
items.desc: Firing, demoting, or punishing someone for reporting an injury or filing a comp claim is illegal in California. The independent attorneys we connect you with work on contingency, so you can ask about your rights without paying anything upfront.

items.question: I was hit on SR-237 while driving a company vehicle. Is that a workplace injury or a car accident?
items.answer: It can be both. Because you were on the job, workers' compensation would typically cover your medical care and a portion of lost wages regardless of fault. If another driver caused the crash, you may also have a separate third-party injury claim against that driver, which follows California's two-year deadline. An attorney can help you pursue both without one undercutting the other.

items.question: Can I sue my employer directly for an injury at a Sunnyvale worksite?
items.answer: In most cases, no. California's workers' compensation system is generally the exclusive remedy against your employer, even if the employer was careless. The exception is when a party other than your employer, such as a subcontractor, the property owner, or the maker of a defective tool, contributed to the injury. That third party can be held responsible through a separate claim.

items.question: I waited a few weeks to tell my employer about the injury. Is it too late?
items.answer: Not necessarily, but you should act now. California asks workers to report an injury to their employer within 30 days, and delays can complicate a comp claim. Reporting in writing as soon as possible protects you, and a connected attorney can help you understand your options if the window has already passed.
